screens.title: Database Performance Tuning and Indexing
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a practical understanding of how databases choose work plans and how indexes change those plans. We'll focus on reading query execution plans with EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE, recognizing costly operations like full table scans and expensive sorts, and selecting effective indexes such as B-tree and composite indexes. You'll also see common pitfalls — over-indexing, functions that prevent index use, and low-cardinality traps — and learn how to maintain statistics so the optimizer makes good decisions. For concrete practice we use an OrderItems table scenario where we'll measure performance before and after creating a composite index on product and date. By the end you should be able to read a plan, propose an index, and validate the result safely in a staging environment. Think of this as the toolkit you'll use when a slow query affects your application: identify the bottleneck, design the index, test the change, and confirm improvement.

screens.title: Query Execution Plan and EXPLAIN
screens.narratorSegment: A query execution plan is the series of operations the database will perform to return your query results. The optimizer considers available indexes, table sizes, join orders, and statistics and builds a plan that minimizes cost. EXPLAIN shows the optimizer's estimated plan without running the query; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and reports actual times and row counts. When you read a plan, focus on expensive nodes such as Seq Scan, Sort, or Nested Loop that process many rows. Look at estimated versus actual rows: large mismatches hint at stale statistics or wrong selectivity assumptions. For example, if EXPLAIN shows a Seq Scan on a large OrderItems table for a query filtering by product_id and date, an index on those columns may eliminate the full scan. A common misconception is trusting estimated cost numbers without checking actual execution; EXPLAIN ANALYZE gives the concrete runtime picture you need to validate changes. Practice by running EXPLAIN first to understand the plan shape, then use EXPLAIN ANALYZE in staging to measure real gains and verify that any index you add is actually being used.

keyIdea.title: Plan basics
keyIdea.text: EXPLAIN shows the optimizer's plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveals actual runtime and is crucial for validation.

content.html:
Definition
Query Execution Plan
The ordered sequence of operations chosen by the optimizer to execute a SQL statement.
Key indicators to read
  • Seq Scan — full table read; costly on large tables.
  • Index Scan — uses an index to locate rows quickly.
  • Nested Loop Join — repeated inner scans for each outer row.
  • Hash/Merge Join — typically better for larger inputs.
Key Takeaway

Always compare estimated and actual rows with EXPLAIN ANALYZE to decide if an index will help.

Example: EXPLAIN ANALYZE (PostgreSQL)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT *
FROM OrderItems
WHERE product_id = 105
  AND item_date >= '2023-01-01'
  AND item_date < '2023-02-01';
Running this in staging will show whether the query used a Seq Scan or an Index Scan. If you see Seq Scan on a large table, an index is a likely remedy.
Misconception: EXPLAIN alone is enough. Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE for true runtime.
Practice: Run EXPLAIN then EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare node timings and row counts.

screens.title: Using EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE safely
screens.narratorSegment: EXPLAIN gives you the optimizer's estimate without running the query, which is safe in production when a query might be expensive. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and returns actual timings and row counts, which is essential in staging to verify improvements. Start with EXPLAIN to get a plan shape: look for Seq Scans, Index Scans, join methods, and sorts. Then, in a controlled environment, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to measure real costs and confirm whether a proposed index changes the node types and reduces time. Pay attention to actual vs estimated rows — large discrepancies indicate inaccurate statistics or selectivity assumptions. Also observe buffer read counts and time spent in sort nodes; an index that covers ORDER BY can eliminate a Sort node entirely. A common pitfall is running EXPLAIN ANALYZE in production without precautions; it can be expensive. Instead, copy the query to staging with similar data distribution, or use EXPLAIN in production for a quick plan shape and EXPLAIN ANALYZE in staging for measurement. Using EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE safely means use explain for quick production checks and explain analyze in staging to measure actual runtime and validate index benefits.. In practical terms, when to use explain vs explain analyze and how to interpret differences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
EXPLAIN → EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Step-by-step: inspect, hypothesize, test, confirm.
  1. Inspect: Run EXPLAIN to see plan nodes and estimates.
  2. Hypothesize: If you see Seq Scan, consider an index on filtered columns.
  3. Test: In staging, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after creating the index.
  4. Confirm: Compare actual times, rows, and node types.
Key Takeaway

EXPLAIN is low-risk; EXPLAIN ANALYZE gives truth but should be used where execution cost is acceptable.

Commands — examples
-- Estimated plan only
EXPLAIN
SELECT * FROM OrderItems WHERE product_id = 105;

-- Execute and show actual times
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM OrderItems WHERE product_id = 105;
Compare estimated row counts with actual row counts in EXPLAIN ANALYZE output. If estimates are far off, run ANALYZE to update statistics and re-evaluate.
Tip: Run ANALYZE periodically to keep statistics fresh.
Warning: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query; avoid on production if the query mutates data or is very expensive.

screens.title: Indexes and How They Work
screens.narratorSegment: An index is a data structure that speeds data retrieval by allowing the database to find rows without scanning the entire table. The common analogy is the index of a book: instead of reading every page, you look up a topic and go directly to the page list. In databases, indexes map column values to row locations. The most common implementation is a B-tree, which supports equality, range queries, and ordering efficiently. Hash indexes excel at pure equality lookups but are poor for ranges and sorting. Clustered indexes determine the physical storage order of rows on disk, making range queries on the clustered key very fast; only one clustered index can exist per table because it defines row order. Non-clustered indexes are separate structures holding keys and pointers to rows; a table can have many of these. Remember that indexes speed reads but slow writes because every insert, update, or delete must also update each affected index. A misconception is thinking more indexes are always better; the right balance is a minimal set that supports frequent read patterns while limiting write overhead.

keyIdea.title: Index trade-off
keyIdea.text: Indexes trade faster reads for slower writes and extra storage; choose them where read benefits outweigh write costs.

content.html:
Concept
What is an Index?
A structure mapping column values to row locations so queries can avoid full table scans.
B-tree: general purpose, supports ranges and ORDER BY.
Hash: fast for equality, not for ranges or ordering.
Clustered: physical row order, one per table.
Non-clustered: pointers to rows, many per table.
Analogy and example
If you query OrderItems for a product and date range, an index on (product_id, item_date) can let the DB locate matching rows with far fewer reads than scanning every row.
Common misconception
Adding indexes for every query pattern seems helpful, but each index increases storage, memory pressure, and write latency. Index selectively.
Key Takeaway

Match index type to query needs: B-tree for ranges and sorts, hash for equality-only lookups.

screens.title: Clustered vs Non-clustered and B-tree vs Hash
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between clustered and non-clustered indexes, or B-tree and hash, depends on query patterns. A clustered index defines the table's physical order; it's ideal when your workload frequently queries ranges on the clustered key because relevant rows are stored together. In contrast, non-clustered indexes are separate lookup structures and work well when you need multiple access paths to a table. B-tree indexes are the default for most workloads because they support equality, range, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY efficiently. Hash indexes are narrower in purpose: they provide fast equality lookups but cannot serve range scans or ordering. A common misstep is creating a hash index hoping to speed many query types; if your queries include ranges or sorts, a B-tree is usually the better choice. Also remember that only one clustered index can exist per table. Practically, design the clustered index on a column used in many range queries or on the primary key if access patterns align, and use non-clustered indexes for selective lookup paths. Clustered vs Non-clustered and B-tree vs Hash means pick clustered index for physical range locality; use b-tree for general queries; use hash only for pure equality hot spots.. In practical terms, when each index type is appropriate and their practical limits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison
Clustered vs Non-clustered
Clustered: physical row order, great for range scans on the key.
Non-clustered: separate structure, multiple per table, useful for many lookup patterns.
One clustered index per table
Many non-clustered indexes allowed
Comparison
B-tree vs Hash
B-tree: supports equality, range queries, ORDER BY and GROUP BY. Good default choice.
Hash: optimized for equality only. Not suitable for ranges or sorting.
Use B-tree for ORDER BY
Use Hash for tight equality hot paths

screens.title: Designing Composite Indexes and Column Order
screens.narratorSegment: A composite index covers multiple columns and is powerful when queries filter or sort on that exact column combination. The order of columns in a composite index matters: place the most selective column or the column used with equality conditions first, and the range or ordering column later. For example, a query filtering product_id = 105 and a date range on item_date benefits from an index on (product_id, item_date). The optimizer can use the first column to quickly narrow results and then apply the range on the second column. Composite indexes can also serve ORDER BY and GROUP BY when the index order matches the sorting order. An incorrect assumption is that any order works; if you flip the columns to (item_date, product_id) you might lose the ability to efficiently satisfy the equality on product_id first. Test composite indexes by running EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after creation to confirm an Index Scan replaced a Seq Scan and whether the Sort node disappears when ordering aligns with the index. Designing Composite Indexes and Column Order means put selective equality columns first in a composite index; place range or ordering columns later to allow efficient lookups and sorts.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Design
Composite Index: Column Order Matters
When queries combine equality and range conditions, order the composite index columns so equality columns come first. This enables efficient index seeks followed by constrained range scans.
Good
CREATE INDEX idx_prod_date ON OrderItems (product_id, item_date);
Why: equality on product_id narrows rows before applying the date range.
Less effective
CREATE INDEX idx_date_prod ON OrderItems (item_date, product_id);
Why: if queries often filter by product_id equality, this ordering may not support index seeks on product_id first.
Always validate with EXPLAIN ANALYZE; the optimizer will only use the index effectively when your query predicates match the index's leading columns.

screens.title: Create and test a composite index
screens.narratorSegment: After measuring the baseline, create a composite B-tree index that matches the query's filter pattern. For the example query filtering by product_id equality and an item_date range, a composite index on (product_id, item_date) is appropriate. Create the index in staging and rerun EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Observe whether the Seq Scan is replaced by an Index Scan or Index Only Scan, and check whether the Sort node disappears if ordering is involved. Compare actual runtime and rows processed: a successful index will reduce the number of heap reads and total execution time. Also note whether the index becomes a covering index — if the query only selects indexed columns, the database may use an Index Only Scan which avoids fetching the table rows. After testing, measure write impacts by running some inserts to see index-maintenance cost. Always create indexes in non-production or during low-traffic windows and monitor resource usage while the index builds on large tables. Create and test a composite index means create the composite index, compare explain analyze outputs, and verify reduced i/o and runtime while checking write overhead.. In practical terms, add an index on (product_id, item_date) and validate improvements with explain analyze. screens.title: Indexing Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Indexing has pitfalls that can reduce overall system performance if not managed carefully. Over-indexing creates many structures to maintain on every write, slowing INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE and consuming disk space. Avoid indexing low-cardinality columns like booleans because the index provides little selectivity. Another frequent issue is applying functions to indexed columns, for example using YEAR(order_date) or wrapping a column in a function inside WHERE; many databases cannot use the index in those cases. Prefer range predicates or rewrite queries to use column ranges so the index can be used. A subtle mistake is assuming an index will be used just because it exists; the optimizer might still choose a full scan when the table is small or statistics suggest a scan is cheaper. Keep statistics up to date with ANALYZE or VACUUM ANALYZE so the optimizer can make correct decisions. The safety practice is to test index changes in staging and measure both read improvements and write regressions before applying to production. screens.title: Statistics, ANALYZE, and Ongoing Tuning
screens.narratorSegment: Optimizers rely on statistics about data distribution to estimate selectivity and cost. If statistics are stale or inaccurate, the optimizer may pick poor plans or ignore an index. Commands like ANALYZE TABLE in MySQL or VACUUM ANALYZE in PostgreSQL update statistics so the optimizer can make informed choices. In this lesson you will build a practical understanding of how databases choose work plans and how indexes change those plans. We'll focus on reading query execution plans with EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE, recognizing costly operations like full table scans and expensive sorts, and selecting effective indexes such as B-tree and composite indexes. You'll also see common pitfalls — over-indexing, functions that prevent index use, and low-cardinality traps — and learn how to maintain statistics so the optimizer makes good decisions. For concrete practice we use an OrderItems table scenario where we'll measure performance before and after creating a composite index on product and date. By the end you should be able to read a plan, propose an index, and validate the result safely in a staging environment. Think of this as the toolkit you'll use when a slow query affects your application: identify the bottleneck, design the index, test the change, and confirm improvement.

In this chapter you will develop practical skills for diagnosing and fixing query performance problems. First, you'll learn to read a query execution plan produced by EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE, recognizing costly operations and interpreting estimated versus actual row counts. Second, you'll identify bottlenecks like full table scans, nested loop joins over large sets, and excessive sorts, and map each to likely fixes such as adding an index or rewriting joins. Third, you will understand the main index types—B-tree, hash, clustered and non-clustered—and when a composite index is appropriate. Finally, you'll apply hands-on steps to test changes safely: run EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after adding an index, compare execution times and plan shapes, and confirm that write overhead remains acceptable. Throughout, you'll practice on a realistic OrderItems scenario so you can transfer these steps directly to staging and production workstreams.

These objectives focus on measurable actions you can perform in a database environment. You will run EXPLAIN ANALYZE against a query on an OrderItems table, read the plan to confirm whether a Seq Scan or Index Scan occurred, and record before-and-after timings. You will create a B-tree index and a composite index suited to the query filter and date range patterns, then rerun EXPLAIN ANALYZE to validate effects on execution time, rows processed, and sorter usage. In addition, you will practice avoiding common mistakes: don't index low-cardinality columns, don't apply functions to indexed columns in WHERE clauses, and weigh the write cost of each new index. Finally, you'll learn to refresh statistics with ANALYZE or VACUUM ANALYZE so the optimizer has accurate distribution data. These are repeatable steps that make performance tuning a controlled, testable workflow.

A query execution plan is the series of operations the database will perform to return your query results. The optimizer considers available indexes, table sizes, join orders, and statistics and builds a plan that minimizes cost. EXPLAIN shows the optimizer's estimated plan without running the query; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and reports actual times and row counts. When you read a plan, focus on expensive nodes such as Seq Scan, Sort, or Nested Loop that process many rows. Look at estimated versus actual rows: large mismatches hint at stale statistics or wrong selectivity assumptions. For example, if EXPLAIN shows a Seq Scan on a large OrderItems table for a query filtering by product_id and date, an index on those columns may eliminate the full scan. A common misconception is trusting estimated cost numbers without checking actual execution; EXPLAIN ANALYZE gives the concrete runtime picture you need to validate changes. Practice by running EXPLAIN first to understand the plan shape, then use EXPLAIN ANALYZE in staging to measure real gains and verify that any index you add is actually being used.

EXPLAIN gives you the optimizer's estimate without running the query, which is safe in production when a query might be expensive. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and returns actual timings and row counts, which is essential in staging to verify improvements. Start with EXPLAIN to get a plan shape: look for Seq Scans, Index Scans, join methods, and sorts. Then, in a controlled environment, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to measure real costs and confirm whether a proposed index changes the node types and reduces time. Pay attention to actual vs estimated rows — large discrepancies indicate inaccurate statistics or selectivity assumptions. Also observe buffer read counts and time spent in sort nodes; an index that covers ORDER BY can eliminate a Sort node entirely. A common pitfall is running EXPLAIN ANALYZE in production without precautions; it can be expensive. Instead, copy the query to staging with similar data distribution, or use EXPLAIN in production for a quick plan shape and EXPLAIN ANALYZE in staging for measurement. An index is a data structure that speeds data retrieval by allowing the database to find rows without scanning the entire table. The common analogy is the index of a book: instead of reading every page, you look up a topic and go directly to the page list. In databases, indexes map column values to row locations. The most common implementation is a B-tree, which supports equality, range queries, and ordering efficiently. Hash indexes excel at pure equality lookups but are poor for ranges and sorting. Clustered indexes determine the physical storage order of rows on disk, making range queries on the clustered key very fast; only one clustered index can exist per table because it defines row order. Non-clustered indexes are separate structures holding keys and pointers to rows; a table can have many of these. Remember that indexes speed reads but slow writes because every insert, update, or delete must also update each affected index. A misconception is thinking more indexes are always better; the right balance is a minimal set that supports frequent read patterns while limiting write overhead.

Choosing between clustered and non-clustered indexes, or B-tree and hash, depends on query patterns. A clustered index defines the table's physical order; it's ideal when your workload frequently queries ranges on the clustered key because relevant rows are stored together. In contrast, non-clustered indexes are separate lookup structures and work well when you need multiple access paths to a table. B-tree indexes are the default for most workloads because they support equality, range, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY efficiently. Hash indexes are narrower in purpose: they provide fast equality lookups but cannot serve range scans or ordering. A common misstep is creating a hash index hoping to speed many query types; if your queries include ranges or sorts, a B-tree is usually the better choice. A composite index covers multiple columns and is powerful when queries filter or sort on that exact column combination. The order of columns in a composite index matters: place the most selective column or the column used with equality conditions first, and the range or ordering column later. The optimizer can use the first column to quickly narrow results and then apply the range on the second column. Composite indexes can also serve ORDER BY and GROUP BY when the index order matches the sorting order. An incorrect assumption is that any order works; if you flip the columns to (item_date, product_id) you might lose the ability to efficiently satisfy the equality on product_id first.
